title: Understanding Yourself Through Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
description: This article introduces the basics of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and shows how core and intermediate beliefs shape automatic thoughts and emotions. Using the metaphor of an apple tree, it explains how internal mindsets influence our perception of events and our reactions. The provided examples demonstrate why the same event can trigger different emotions in different people.

texts: In today's world, filled with stress and uncertainty, psychological well-being is more important than ever.
Millions of people face difficulties every day—ranging from mild discomfort and anxiety to serious conditions such as depression, neurosis, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and others.
These challenges can significantly impact quality of life, making it hard to enjoy everyday moments, build warm relationships, and move toward your goals.
If you are reading these lines and feel like something inside is preventing you from living life to the fullest—you are not alone, and this is natural.
Even the most successful and outwardly calm people experience destructive mindsets and internal barriers.
Often, their roots go back to childhood, shaped by the influence of traumatic events or unfavorable circumstances.
It is important to remember: having these difficulties does not make you "broken"—it is a part of the human experience.
If you are looking for change, we invite you on a fascinating journey into the world of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT).
This effective approach helps you understand yourself better and provides tools to manage your thoughts and emotions.
In this chapter, we will begin by introducing the fundamental ideas of the method.
<q author="Rebecca Walker">Our thoughts shape our perception, and that perception determines how we live.</q>
Whether your difficulties seem minor or cause significant distress—from temporary low moods to long-standing symptoms: CBT can be a valuable resource.
Right now, we will offer a simplified model of the key concept, and in the following chapters, we will explore it in more detail.
In Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, the mind is conceptually described through three levels: core beliefs, intermediate beliefs (rules), and automatic thoughts.
The key idea of CBT is that our well-being and feelings depend on how we think.
<important>From this comes the core principle: when we notice and consciously correct our thinking, life becomes more stable and productive.</important>
This is a brief summary of the essence of CBT, but there are many more important details ahead that we look forward to sharing with you.
To make it more visual, let's imagine an apple tree.
In this metaphor, the roots are the core beliefs: fundamental assumptions about yourself, the world, and others.
They are formed by early experiences and are often unconscious. Examples: "I am unworthy of love," "The world is a dangerous place."
The trunk represents intermediate beliefs—the rules and mindsets that guide us day after day.
They are based on core beliefs and direct our reactions. Examples: "If I am not perfect, I won't be loved," "To survive, I must always be on guard."
The canopy represents automatic thoughts: quick, spontaneous reactions to events.
These are like the fruit on the tree—they can be "healthy" or "rotten." Examples: "I'm late—so I must leave earlier next time" or "I'm late—so I'm a failure."
Each of us has our own "tree," and we view every event through its lens.
Therefore, the same situation can trigger completely different emotions in different people—meaning is assigned through one's own beliefs.
This is how a wide spectrum of emotional reactions is formed, even in response to seemingly identical events.
Let's look at an example. Two colleagues received the same feedback at work:
Maria: since childhood, she has developed the core belief "I am not good enough."

Her intermediate belief: "To be valued, I must be flawless." Upon receiving criticism, she thinks: "I messed everything up, my boss is disappointed, I'm going to lose my job." The result—fear, anxiety, and exhaustion.
Kristina: she has a different core belief—“I am capable of learning and growing."

Her intermediate belief: "Criticism is an opportunity to get better." After hearing the feedback, she thinks: "My boss pointed out my weaknesses—this will help me improve my work." The result—calmness, motivation, and a readiness to correct mistakes.
So, the event is exactly the same—feedback from a boss.
But the reactions are opposites—because of the differences in core and intermediate beliefs.
CBT helps you notice and change these beliefs so you can react more constructively and maintain emotional balance.
<important>Since everyone has their own "tree model," even identical situations are perceived differently.</important>
In response to them, automatic thoughts are born, which in turn influence emotions and behavior.
We will certainly discuss the connection between thoughts, emotions, and behavior in more detail in the following chapters.
In this chapter, we have sketched out the big picture, so don't worry if you still have many questions: we will return to these ideas and break them down further.
We suggest approaching this material with openness and a readiness to experiment. Use these techniques in practice—and let your life become fuller, more joyful, and more harmonious.
